item.title: Scientists get clearest view yet of a spreading seafloor
item.description: A rare eruption in the Indian Ocean let researchers capture one of the clearest views yet of a seafloor spreading event

item.title: Seeding clouds with seawater could prevent a super El Niño
item.description: A modelling study suggests marine cloud brightening could shade the eastern Pacific and reduce a global temperature spike from El Niño, but there could be unexpected consequences

item.title: You Can Now Get a PhD in China by Inventing a Product Instead of Writing a 100-page Dissertation
item.description: China is tired of PhD students writing papers that no one reads and is demanding they build real products instead.

item.title: Can geoengineering blunt El Niño’s fury?
item.description: Marine cloud brightening could cool part of the Pacific and weaken extreme El Niños, simulations suggest. But the approach could have risks.

item.title: Can we geoengineer ourselves out of an El Niño year?
item.description: A controversial geoengineering proposal suggests that brightening clouds off South America could weaken a burgeoning El Niño, but major technical and ethical questions remain

item.title: ESPN Is Bringing Back the World Series of Poker, This Time with AI That Spots Players Bluffing
item.description: AI is learning to spot poker bluffs by watching the tiny tells players try to hide.

item.title: AI Cracked the Rules of a Lost Roman Board Game, and It’s Unlike Anything We Expected
item.description: You can now play the lost Roman board game called Ludus Coriovalli that was discovered in a museum.

item.title: Snoring May Be Both a Symptom and a Cause of Sleep Apnea
item.description: Snoring vibrations may weaken throat muscles by disrupting cellular energy.

item.title: Turning Off a Protein Called ‘Mitch’ Made Mice Virtually Immune to Obesity. Scientists Just Tested It In Human Cells
item.description: Scientists found a cellular switch that raises energy use and blocks new fat cells.

item.title: Our fertility window could be extended by making ovaries softer
item.description: A drug that softens the ovaries helped mice and rats conceive more easily at an older age, and produce more pups

item.title: Why subsidies won’t work for EV battery recycling in China
item.description:
Subsidies aren’t enough to develop the battery recycling sector and handle a wave from retired electric vehicles, writes Zhang Yijun

The post Why subsidies won’t work for EV battery recycling in China appeared first on Dialogue Earth.

item.title: Occam’s razor has lost its edge. Can we sharpen our search for truth?
item.description: Seeking out the simplest, most elegant explanations has served scientists well for centuries, but cognitive scientist Marina Dubova’s experiments are revealing better ways to uncover reality

item.title: RFK, Jr. is turning his attention to the U.S. Preventive Services Taskforce
item.description: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force is an independent group that offers guidance on what health screenings and medications health insurance should cover

item.title: Why ‘Neil the seal’ is unleashing chaos in Tasmania
item.description: This one-ton elephant seal has gone viral for smashing into cars and infrastructure, but biologists have a more poignant explanation for his behavior

item.description: A best-yet measurement of one of general relativity’s most mind-boggling effects is “another feather in Einstein’s cap”

item.description: Delivered by PolitePaul service

item.title: Detecting hidden nuclear weapons in space may be possible using cosmic rays
item.description: For almost 60 years, a global ban on nuclear weapons in space has held up. But the growing number of satellites and increasing geopolitical tension has scientists worried the moratorium could fail

item.title: Older adults are at risk in heat waves, but it’s not just age: How public systems and policies are failing them
item.description: The challenge is not a lack of evidence. It is a lack of urgency.

item.title: Why Schrödinger's 1944 classic What Is Life? still feels prescient
item.description: Pioneer of quantum mechanics Erwin Schrödinger's look at living organisms is one of the most influential popular-science books of the 20th century. So how does it hold up today, asks Karmela Padavic-Callaghan

item.title: Two Old Drugs May Help Protect the Brain After Stroke by Triggering a Hibernation-Like State
item.description: Two old drugs may buy the brain time after a stroke.

item.title: Lambs born via IVF using highly immature eggs in major breakthrough
item.description: Lambs have been born using an experimental form of IVF that coaxes immature eggs to become mature ones. This could boost the number of eggs available for fertilisation and improve IVF success rates

item.title: Two 500-Year-Old Freeze-Dried Potatoes Show How the Inca Empire Fed People Across Peru
item.description: Found inside a broken clay jar, the rare potato remains survived centuries in Peru's desert-like conditions.

item.title: Dolphins In The Adriatic Are Chasing Trawlers for Scraps Because Their Sea Is Running Out Of Food
item.description: Scientists tracked more than 17,700 kilometers of fishing activity to uncover a dramatic shift in dolphin behavior.

item.title: Why more extreme rain could mean more shark bites
item.description: As rainfall intensifies with climate change, waste flushed out to sea could attract more sharks, putting beachgoers at risk

item.title: The Oceans Just Broke a Heat Record and El Niño Could Push Them Even Higher
item.description: El Niño and climate change are pushing sea temperatures into record territory.

item.title: The allergy culprit histamine also boosts our memory
item.description: A drug that raises levels of histamine – the chemical that causes allergy symptoms – in the brain boosts our memory by around 10 per cent

item.title: British First Fleet Likely Brought Smallpox to Australia and the Actual Toll May Have Been Millions
item.description: Researchers say British colonization of Australia may have killed millions after smallpox arrived with the First Fleet

item.title: How extreme heat affects the body – and the best ways to cope
item.description: A short spell in a heat chamber at the University of Brighton showed Alec Luhn that his body is not adapted to high temperatures – but regular exposure can train the body to respond more effectively

item.title: International timekeepers to vote on changing the leap second to a leap hour
item.description: To align Universal Coordinated Time with Earth’s rotation, a second occasionally gets added to the year. That may change in 2027

item.title: I want to see a prison-to-PhD pipeline
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01673-8

Ryan Rising creates programmes that help people who have been incarcerated to access academic opportunities.

item.title: How to advance revolutionary science: high turnover, high risk and a licence to fail
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02090-7

Kathleen Fisher reveals the recipe for funding innovative science that she brings to the UK Advanced Research and Invention Agency.

item.title: Those who forget
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01933-7

Clarity of thought.

item.title: Nukes in space? Orbital detector could sniff out warheads
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02141-z

A shoebox-sized detector satellite could identify the telltale signal of a hidden nuclear device — plus, how Indigenous plant knowledge is under threat.

item.title: Observation of Floquet rotational super-radiance
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10725-y

A Floquet regime of rotational super-radiance has been observed in a spatiotemporally modulated ring network of resonators.

item.title: In vivo feasibility study of humanoid robots in surgery
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10796-x

A systematic evaluation shows that contemporary humanoid robots can perform laparoscopic surgical tasks through teleoperation, highlighting both their promise and key technical challenges before clinical deployment.

item.title: Single-phase gradient-solvation-electrolyte-stabilized Li metal batteries
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10732-z

A targeted ligand anti-solvent is incorporated into an anion-rich ether-based electrolyte and used to achieve lithium metal batteries with a long cycle life, high energy density and high capacity retention.

item.title: Non-genotoxic transplantation and in vivo selection through epitope editing
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10737-8

Epitope editing of KIT enables antibody-based, non-genotoxic conditioning that selectively enriches therapeutic BCL11A-edited haematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, supports durable engraftment, preserves clonal diversity and enhances induction of fetal haemoglobin, a therapeutic approach for conditions such as sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia.

item.title: Architecture of the 8 MDa Hdr–Vhu–Fwd super-assembly in class I methanogens
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10744-9

The structure of the Hdr–Vhu–Fwd super-assembly reveals a lineage-specific and modular 8 MDa complex with the ability to adapt to diverse anaerobic niches.

item.title: Reinforcement learning control of quantum error correction
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10759-2

By integrating reinforcement learning with quantum error correction, a quantum computer continuously self-calibrates during computation, achieving record logical error rates and enhanced resilience to drift.

item.title: Large language models can predict the results of social science experiments
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10742-x

Large language models can be used to estimate the results of social science experiments about as accurately as a group of human forecasters—even for experiments published after the models were trained—although they tended to overestimate effect sizes.

item.title: Ancient feeding-related neuropeptides regulate alloparenting in ants
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10747-6

Pharmacological screening and behavioural assays in ants identify two specific neuropeptides that have key and opposite effects in regulating brood care, and that link nutritional state to age-dependent changes in parenting behaviour.

item.title: Anatomy of a seafloor spreading event captured by in situ seismogeodesy
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10785-0

By combining hydroacoustic, direct-path ranging and bottom-pressure measurements, in situ observations of a rifting event at a segment of the Southeast Indian Ridge are reported, providing insight into seafloor spreading events on yearly timescales.

item.title: Computational approaches and the future of urban crime research
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10622-4

This Review examines the opportunities and challenges introduced by new datasets and computational techniques in urban crime research, and outlines future directions for leveraging these advances effectively.

item.title: Reconfigurable mmWave microchips co-integrating hBN switches on GaN
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10761-8

Radio-frequency switches made from two-dimensional layered hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) were co-integrated on gallium nitride (GaN) microchips to build programmable millimetre-wave (mmWave) monolithic microwave integrated circuits suitable for 6G hardware.

item.title: Air-permeable hydrogels through viscoelastic phase separation of aerogels
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10712-3

Viscoelastic phase separation is used to fabricate non-collapsible, air-rich networks in high-water-content hydrogels containing silica aerogel beads, allowing air to permeate through the material and enabling a tenfold increase in oxygen permeability over pristine hydrogels.

item.title: Verification of the Outer Space Treaty with cosmic protons
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10783-2

By observing the neutrons induced by spallation from protons in the inner Van Allen radiation belts using widely available sensor technologies, the detection of a thermonuclear weapon carried by a space satellite is possible.

item.title: Aneuploidy selects for the acquisition of driver genes in breast cancer
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10752-9

Screening of chromosome arm-level aneuploidies uncovers that these alterations select for specific basal-like breast cancer driver genes, including PLGRKT, an oncogene whose tumour-promoting activity is associated with highly stress-resistant mitochondria and enhanced detoxification of reactive oxygen species.

item.title: Universal cell embedding provides a foundation model for cell biology
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10689-z

The universal cell embedding foundation model learns to capture the organization and variation of cells by training on 36 million cells from hundreds of experiments, dozens of tissues and eight species.

item.title: LARES-2 satellite measures frame-dragging effect around the Earth
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10715-0

Using LARES-2, LAGEOS and GRACE satellites, researchers measured Earth’s frame-dragging with unprecedented precision, strongly confirming general relativity, constraining alternative gravity theories, and improving measurements of Earth’s tides.

item.title: Chromatin landscape and epigenetic heterogeneity of acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10703-4

An ATAC-seq-based approach is used to classify acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) into 16 epigenomic subgroups, and provides insight into the role of non-genetic mechanisms in determining pathogenesis, clinical behaviour and drug sensitivity in this disease.

item.title: Diet–microbiome synergy underlies obesity-associated immunotherapy efficacy
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10750-x

Diet shapes obesity-associated therapeutic responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors through gut microbial metabolism and host anti-tumour immunity, demonstrated in mouse custom-diet models and human-to-mouse fecal microbiota transplantation experiments.

item.title: Intergenerational mobility fosters innovation in Europe
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10736-9

The EUROPE-IGM-ATLAS reveals spatiotemporal trends that characterize the changing geography of opportunity in Europe and its relationship with regional innovation.

item.title: An intrinsic cytoskeletal oscillator establishes neuronal polarity
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10755-6

The ARP2/3 complex works together with actomyosin in an oscillatory program at the soma to govern neuronal polarization.

item.title: The forest of knowledge under global change
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10741-y

The biocultural heritage of the Amazon, its plant species, plant services and cultures are at risk from climate change.

item.title: Regenerating people–nature relationships to counter biocultural erosion in the Amazon
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01874-1

Rebuilding the reciprocal care-oriented relationships between Amazonian Indigenous peoples and nature could address the predicted effects of climate change on biodiversity.

item.title: Volcanoes and wildfires contributed to increased stratospheric humidification
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02011-8

Observations from satellites and climate-model simulations show that moderate volcanic eruptions and extreme wildfires have humidified the stratosphere since 2005. The aerosol-mediated effects of these eruptions and fires explain about one-third of the observed stratospheric water-vapour trend, a contribution similar to that of surface warming.

item.title: Ocean floor witnessed splitting apart for the first time — releasing lava
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02139-7

Scientists observed a mid-ocean ridge widen in real time, recording several metres of sea-floor motion and huge lava outflows.

item.title: Breast cancer driver genes found by screening chromosome aberrations in vivo
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02014-5

Cancer genomes are unstable, often experiencing gains or losses of whole chromosomes or chromosome arms — changes known as aneuploidies. Experiments in mouse models of breast cancer reveal that these instabilities harbour one or two prevalent genes that drive cancer and that bypass the need to accumulate aneuploidies; they also require an intact microenvironment to produce their effects.

item.title: Judicious use of LLMs could speed up progress in the social sciences
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01875-0

Large language models could advance experiments in the social sciences, but fundamental questions remain about how they should be used to support research.

item.title: Sea-floor spreading captured by undersea observatory
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01943-5

A sea-floor monitoring experiment observed oceanic crust being created between two tectonic plates — the first in situ measurement of this phenomenon.

item.title: Nuclear weapons lurking in space could be tracked down by satellites
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-01944-4

A nuclear weapon orbiting Earth would emit neutrons through its interactions with the planet’s space radiation environment, and these could be detected by satellites.

item.title: Nobel-winning chemist leaves US to direct AI materials lab in China
item.description:
Nature, Published online: 08 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02143-x

Omar Yaghi’s move comes amid cuts to US science and a campaign in China to recruit top international talent.
